name: Wei Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior office administrator at Kowalczyk Builders, a family building firm with about sixty people. I book material deliveries to sites, file the health and safety forms, chase subcontractor invoices and keep the site diaries in order. Twice a week I drive out to a site with paperwork, which I enjoy, because you see the actual houses going up. The office is two portakabins joined together, and it's freezing in January.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pricing, mostly. I don't understand the quantity sheets yet, and Ray (the senior estimator) has to explain them twice. I use the AI sometimes to tidy an email, nothing more. I bought a small flat last year with savings and a bit of help from my parents, and I've still got about seven months put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about nothing. Builders still need bricks, and bricks still need someone to order them. I'd say that at five-a-side and get a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. The office might lose a bit of typing, but Mr Kowalczyk likes paper copies of everything anyway. My job would stay the same, and I could keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Ray to teach me the quantity sheets properly, maybe one evening a week. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month. And I'd use the AI for emails now that everyone else does too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you already, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building goes up and down with interest rates. If people stop buying houses, the firm slows, and the office feels it. But Mr Kowalczyk kept everyone on in the last slow patch, so I trust him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does learning the quantity sheets matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's the real skill in our office. Anyone can file forms. If I can price a building job, I've got a trade, even if it's a desk trade.

I'd joke about it at **five-a-side** football.
think: Mr Kowalczyk likes **paper copies**, so the office barely changes.
My job stays the same and I can keep **learning**.
do: Ask Ray to teach me **quantity sheets** one evening a week.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** a little each month.
Use AI for **emails** now that everyone does.

fieldNote: He sees **estimating** as the real skill worth learning.
**Interest rates** are the firm's existing pressure, not AI.
He **trusts the owner**, who kept staff on in a slow patch.

steps.text: Learn quantity sheets from Ray one evening a week
Overpay the flat mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has its new machines and people adjust. Firms should train their own people, like apprenticeships, rather than waiting for the government. I'd say that at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office side of my job shrinks a lot. Ordering, invoices, forms, that's what it does. But building firms will always need someone on site who knows the job, and I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen the new tools working for other firms, I'd ask Mr Kowalczyk to move me towards site work, maybe as an assistant site manager. I'd do the site safety course, which the firm pays for. And I'd learn the new ordering software, because it's easier to move if you can use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I'd feel I had a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda, who does the accounts and has been there twenty years. She's great at it, but software would do most of it. I'd hope Mr Kowalczyk finds her something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the site really safer for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than the portakabin, yes. Robots in muddy building sites are a long way off. I'd rather have muddy boots than no job.

say: Every generation has **new machines**, and people adjust.
Firms should train their own people through **apprenticeships**, not wait for government.
think: The **office side** of my job shrinks a lot: ordering, invoices and forms.
Building firms will always need someone **on site** who knows the job.
do: Ask to move towards **assistant site manager**.
Learn the new **ordering software** once proven.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but with a **path** ahead.
S1.quote: Robots in muddy building sites are a long way off. I'd rather have muddy boots than no job.
fieldNote: He shifts **toward the site** because hands-on work lags.
He waits for **proof** from other firms before moving.
He's more worried for a **long-serving colleague** than himself.

steps.text: Ask Mr Kowalczyk for an assistant site manager role
Take the firm-paid site safety course
Learn the new ordering software once other firms use it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people should look after their own, family first. I'd say firms will need to keep good workers, so be a good worker. I'd not want government handouts to become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the office part of my job goes by 2028. The site part lasts until about 2031, when the robots come. So I'd have three years outdoors, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight away to go full time on site, even at less pay, and start a bricklaying or carpentry apprenticeship. I'd keep the flat and stop overpaying the mortgage, so I hold more cash. I'd talk to my dad, who did joinery years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to worried. My chest would tighten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of a trade, then robots. Is it worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Three years of wages is three years, and I'd be learning something real. After that, someone has to manage the robots on site, and they'd want someone who knows building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say get your hands dirty, son, a trade never hurts. Then my dad would show me how to plane a door in his garage. That would actually help.

say: Firms will keep **good workers**, so be one, without **handouts** becoming normal.
think: The **office part** of my job at Kowalczyk Builders goes by **2028**.
Site work lasts until robots arrive around **2031**, then I don't know.
do: Go **full time on site**, even at lower pay.
Stop overpaying the mortgage to hold **more cash**.
feel: **Uneasy** turning to **worried**, with a tight chest.
S2.quote: My dad would say get your hands dirty, son, a trade never hurts. Then my dad would show me how to plane a door in his garage.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** to buy three years in a trade.
His **father's joinery** is a real, practical resource.
He thinks someone who knows building will be needed to **manage robots**.

steps.text: Move full time to site work at Kowalczyk Builders
Start a carpentry apprenticeship this year
Stop mortgage overpayments and hold the cash
Learn joinery from his dad in the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to learn a trade properly, so get on with it. Apprenticeships, family help, hard work. Not much to argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd manage. Five years is enough to finish a carpentry apprenticeship and get some years in. I'd be 32 when the office work goes, already on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the carpentry apprenticeship in the first year, with Mr Kowalczyk's blessing. I'd keep a few office days while I trained, so the pay doesn't drop too much. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage, so the flat is mostly mine by the time robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. A bit of a knot about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 35, with a trade and a flat that's mostly paid off. That's a decent place to stand, even if the work changes. I'd rather own my home than have savings in the bank when the robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I saw it working. For pricing jobs, it would help me a lot. But I'd use it alongside the trade, not instead of it.

say: Five years is time to **learn a trade properly**.
**Apprenticeships**, family help and hard work are the answer.
think: I'd finish a **carpentry apprenticeship** before office work goes in 2031.
At **32** I'd already be on site, with years in.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** in year one with the owner's blessing.
Keep a few **office days** while training.
S3.quote: I'd rather own my home than have savings in the bank when the robots come in 2034.
fieldNote: Five years makes his trade plan **realistic**.
Owning his **flat outright** is his security goal.
He'd use AI **alongside** a trade, not instead of it.

steps.text: Start a carpentry apprenticeship at Kowalczyk Builders in year one
Keep two office days a week while training
Overpay the mortgage to clear most of the flat by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody should be complaining. Learn a trade, raise a family, pay your way. That's how my parents did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Ten years gives me time to learn estimating properly, get on site, and maybe start a family. By 2036 I'd be 37, and probably running jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the office a couple more years and learn pricing from Ray. Then I'd move to site management, using AI tools once they're proven. I'd pay off a good chunk of the flat and maybe propose to my girlfriend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of uneasiness I'd keep to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your girlfriend? You hadn't mentioned her.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia (my girlfriend), we've been together two years. She's a dental nurse, which is hands-on, so I'd feel better about her than about my desk. Ten years would let us plan things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the uneasiness you'd keep to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and miss the moment. People in building talk about the last recession like it came out of nowhere. I don't want to be that person.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so nobody should complain.
Learn a trade, raise a family and **pay your way**.
think: I'd have time to **learn estimating** and move on site.
By **2036** I'd be 37 and probably running jobs.
do: Learn **pricing** from Ray over a couple of years.
Move into **site management** using proven AI tools.
Pay down the **flat** and propose to Sofia.
S4.quote: People in building talk about the last recession like it came out of nowhere. I don't want to be that person.
fieldNote: A decade fits his **steady** pace: learn, then move.
His private fear is **complacency**, missing the moment like builders in the last recession.

steps.text: Learn job pricing from Ray over two years
Move into site management using proven AI tools
Propose to Sofia and plan a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years on site and then robots, with no time to settle anything. What would help is firms like ours running proper apprenticeships for adults, and family being close by.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the bosses. Mr Kowalczyk's choices matter more to me than anything the government does. A good owner keeps people on.

headlineQuote: Builders still need bricks, and bricks still need someone to order them.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** junior admin at Kowalczyk Builders, a family building firm, still learning to price jobs.
He owns a **small flat** and has seven months saved.
He uses AI now and then and waits for **proof** before trusting tools.
Under each scenario he heads **toward the site** and a carpentry trade.
He believes in **apprenticeships**, family help and a good owner over government support.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, with only three years of site work before **robots**.
